newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico resumes processing sorghum import permits.
newsitem.headline: Mexico resumes processing sorghum import permits.

text.p: Mexican authorities have resumed processing phytosanitary permits for sorghum imports from the United States at normal speeds, trade sources said Tuesday.
"The situation has started to become normal again," Ricardo Celma, director general of the Mexican office of the U.S. Feeds Grains Council, told Reuters.

Mexican authorities, although never officially recognising the move, started to hold up the processing of permits two weeks ago in what trade saw as a temporary import ban on U.S. sorghum until national stocks of the feed grain were sold.

The sorghum saga was provoked by national producers who have found difficulty selling national ssorghum at profits with stocks seen at levels around 2 million tonnes from 1996 and dwindling international prices.

Sources said the outcry was such from national end users that the government called a meeting of producers and the trade to discuss the issue and clarify the stance of Department of Food Hygiene, a branch of the Agriculture Ministry.
Government officials said there was no official stoppage in the processing of permits but that the problem had been caused by an "excess of work".

Sources said strong representation was made at the meeting with government officials from the Association of Farm Sector Suppliers,, known as APSP from its Spanish initials, which groups the biggest players in the Mexican grains sector.

Currently the president of the group is Arturo Enrique from Buenos Aires-based Bunge. Local offices of Cargill, Continental Grain Co. and Archer Daniels Midland (ADM) are also members of the suppliers association.
Delays in delivering phytosanitary certificates had reached up to 30 days in same cases from the normal processing practice of five days, sources said.

"There are very few certificates held up now," said one trade source who asked to remain anonymous, adding that those that were still in the backlog were for small importers and exporters and not the big guns.

The temporary import ban, which some merchandisers accused the government of putting up non-tariff barriers in violation of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), caused headches for those traders with pending contacts to fullfill.
--Chris Aspin, Mexico City newsroom (525) 7289530. E-mail at chris.aspin@reuters.com
